content: If dispersible fixed-dose combinations are unavailable and oral liquids must be used, it is recommended to transition children to solid oral dosage forms as soon as feasible. When children must use adult formulations, careful attention is required to prevent underdosing or overdosing. Splitting unscored tablets should be avoided, as uniform distribution of the active drug cannot be guaranteed in the fragments. Certain tablets, such as heat-stable formulations of LPV/r or ATV, are manufactured using specialized embedded matrix technology (proprietary melt extrusion) to stabilize heat-labile drug molecules. These tablets must not be cut, split, dissolved, chewed, or crushed, as this can lead to variable bioavailability if not swallowed whole. Additionally, differences in morning and evening dosing should be avoided whenever possible. Children should be weighed at every clinic visit, and their medication doses adjusted as they grow or their weight changes. National treatment programs should consider the regulatory and local availability of specific dosage forms when developing treatment recommendations for children. Research is ongoing to establish dosing guidelines for antiretroviral (ARV) medications in newborns, infants, and young children. Age indications for each drug are based on current evidence and will be updated as new recommendations emerge. For infants younger than four weeks, dosing adjustments are necessary due to their reduced ability to metabolize and excrete medications. For infants at least four weeks old but weighing less than 3 kg, the immaturity of renal and hepatic elimination pathways is less concerning, but uncertainties remain regarding appropriate ARV dosing for preterm and low-birth-weight infants. Efavirenz (EFV) is not recommended for children under three years of age or weighing less than 10 kg, as more data is needed to guide its use in this group. Atazanavir (ATV) is approved for children aged three months and older, and its single-strength capsules should always be administered with 100 mg of ritonavir (RTV) across all weight bands. ATV powder formulations allow administration to infants and children as young as three months, with specific dosing guidelines based on weight. Tenofovir (TDF) is approved for children aged two years and older, with a target dose of 8 mg/kg or 200 mg/m² (maximum 300 mg). The Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group has harmonized TDF dosing with WHO weight bands to reduce the number of strengths required. Nevirapine (NVP) dose escalation with a half-dose for two weeks when initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) is still recommended to avoid toxicity from high initial NVP levels. However, recent secondary analyses suggest that younger children may have a lower risk of toxicity, and starting with a full dose may be considered. More definitive evidence is expected from ongoing trials. LPV/r liquid formulations require a cold chain for transport and storage, while heat-stable LPV/r tablets must be swallowed whole and not split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. LPV/r pellets should not be used for infants younger than three months. Raltegravir (RAL) granules are approved for children as young as four weeks, but their feasibility and acceptability in resource-limited settings remain under investigation. The bioequivalence of RAL chewable tablets dispersed in liquid is being explored, and further guidance will be provided as evidence becomes available. There is limited experience with initiating treatment in newborns under two weeks of age, with few pharmacokinetic data available to guide accurate dosing for drugs other than AZT during this period of rapid renal and liver maturation. LPV/r solution should not be given to infants under two weeks of age, and its use in preterm infants is not recommended until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age. This guidance will be updated as more evidence becomes available. Recent years have seen the development of improved ARV formulations, such as dispersible, scored fixed-dose combination tablets, which have simplified HIV care delivery for children in low-income settings. However, the proliferation of options has led to a multiplicity of formulations across regimens and weight bands, complicating procurement and supply chain management. The Interagency Task Team on the Prevention and Treatment of HIV Infection in Pregnant Women, Mothers, and Children provides formulary guidance to programs on selecting optimal ARV drugs for children. The current optimal formulary includes nine products delivering recommended firstand second-line regimens across all pediatric weight bands. This formulary is routinely revised to align with updated WHO guidelines and available products. The Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group continues to emphasize the urgent need for fixed-dose combination formulations to provide recommended first-line regimens, such as LPV/r-containing solid forms for younger children and EFV + ABC + 3TC fixed-dose combinations for children aged 3–10 years. The availability of co-formulated ATV/r and DRV/r in heat-stable fixed-dose combinations is critical for treatment sequencing and scaling up secondand third-line therapies. WHO will continue to work with pharmaceutical partners to simplify prescribing, dispensing, and dosing guidance to accelerate ART scale-up for children.
